**The papers don't answer this.** None of them mention India or any country-specific policy, infrastructure, or market conditions, so they can't tell you whether a battery passport is feasible there.

What one paper (Bai et al., *Materials Today* 2020, "mattod-2020") does offer is the general concept, its requirements and its obstacles. You could use these as criteria when looking at India yourself.

**What the passport is meant to do**
- The authors propose a "Battery Identity Global Passport" (BIGP). It would carry each battery's chemistry, origin, state of health and chain of custody, which recyclers would read to sort batteries automatically (p. 8).
- They suggest it could be a digital chip identifying the battery "at the cradle (manufacturers) and at the gate (recyclers)" (p. 10).
- Simpler identification already exists or has been proposed: labels, QR codes and RFID tags, an SAE label for EV packs, and a US DOE-funded blockchain project (Everledger) to trace battery lifecycles (p. 8).

**Obstacles the authors identify**
- Manufacturers may not want to share proprietary cathode and electrolyte formulations. Stakeholders and policymakers would need agreements between manufacturers and recyclers (p. 8).
- The concept "will have to be globally implemented." Otherwise the complex global flow of batteries "may jeopardize the chances to recycle Li-ion batteries in responsible and profitable ways" (p. 10).
- Recycling in general is held back by a lack of collection regulations and policies, weak collection infrastructure, transport costs, and safety issues in storage and shipping (pp. 2–3).
- From lead-acid recycling, the authors take these lessons: the industry should work proactively with regulators, set up reverse distribution systems to collect spent batteries, and move toward standardized designs (p. 3).
- Coordinated action among academia, industry, governments, investors and policymakers is described as critical (p. 9).

So the paper treats feasibility anywhere as depending on regulation, data-sharing agreements, collection infrastructure and international coordination. Whether India has or is building these is outside what these documents cover.
question: Is battery passport really possible in India
